abstract: ABSTRACT Background Autoimmune hepatitis (AIH) may be difficult to diagnose and distinguish clinically and biochemically from other chronic liver diseases like metabolic dysfunction‐associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD). Aims To identify pathways involved in the pathogenesis and identify disease‐specific biomarkers of AIH. Methods We recruited 19 newly diagnosed patients with AIH, 17 with MASLD, and 19 healthy controls. Liver tissue and plasma were collected, and untargeted mass‐spectrometry‐based proteomics was performed. For classification of AIH versus MASLD and healthy, machine learning analyses were performed employing logistic regression models on liver and plasma proteome data. Findings were validated using data from the United Kingdom Biobank (UKB). Results We identified 7632 liver and 556 plasma proteins with 2521 liver and 227 plasma proteins differing between AIH and healthy, including 56 overlapping. Metabolic dysregulation and systemic immune activation characterised the AIH liver and plasma proteome, respectively. Plasma proteome profiling enabled classification of AIH from MASLD and healthy with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.91 (0.09 SD). Validation in the UKB was possible for 8 of 20 diagnostic proteins and showed consistent directional changes. Three proteins (C7, ICAM1, cAST) were significantly different between AIH and MASLD/healthy in unadjusted analyses, and 6 of 8 proteins (C7, ICAM1, cAST, IGFBP3, TIMP1, TTR) were significantly different when adjusting for age and sex. Conclusions Clinical proteomic analyses of paired liver‐plasma samples from patients with AIH enabled high diagnostic potential. Proteomics may constitute a novel non‐invasive diagnostic tool for AIH if validated in larger, age‐ and sex‐matched cohorts. Clinical Trial Number: NCT05335603

Proteomics Profiling and Machine Learning Modelling
Liver and plasma samples were lysed with lysis buffer, and peptides analysed by EvoSep‐Bruker timsTOF instrument (Figure
1C,D
). Raw liver and plasma mass spectrometry files were processed using Spectronaut and DIA‐NN, respectively (Figure
1E
). Intensity values representing label‐free quantifications (LFQs, i.e., relative concentrations) were log2‐transformed, proteins with less than 70% of valid values in at least one group were removed, and missing values were imputed using the MinProb approach [
23
].
To address our first aim—understanding disease pathophysiology—we performed differential abundance analysis comparing patients with AIH to healthy controls only. This analysis was performed in R version 4.3.2 with the Limma package (3.58.1) which fits a linear model [
24
,
25
] (Figure
1E
). A protein was considered differentially abundant if a false discovery rate adjusted
p
value by Benjamini–Hochberg was < 0.05.
For our second aim—identification of diagnostic biomarkers for AIH—we performed machine learning using the online platform OmicLearn [
26
] to discover protein panels that were able to distinguish AIH from both MASLD and healthy controls combined (Figure
1E
). Logistic regression was applied with a repeated stratified cross‐validation approach. Several models were tested: (1) the predictive value of enzymatically measured (standard biochemistry) alanine aminotransferase (ALT); (2) plasma proteome; (3) plasma proteome and ALT combined; (4) liver proteome; (5) liver proteome and ALT combined; (6) plasma and liver proteome; (7) plasma and liver proteome combined with ALT. Model performances were evaluated with area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (ROC AUC), area under the curve of the precision– recall curve (PR AUC), sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV), negative predictive value (NPV) and accuracy. Results are reported as the mean of all individual splits. For a detailed explanation of the performance metrics, please see Table
S2
.
In addition to the primary analyses, we performed sensitivity analyses both for the mechanistic and biomarker discovery aims by excluding patients with cirrhosis to assess the potential effect of advanced fibrosis. Furthermore, to investigate whether the observed proteomic alterations were specific to AIH rather than reflecting liver injury in general, we conducted a differential abundance analysis comparing AIH with MASLD. For the mechanistic analysis of AIH versus healthy, we additionally performed differential abundance analyses adjusting for age and sex to evaluate the potential influence of these demographic factors on the proteomic differences observed.
2.2
Validation in United Kingdom Biobank
To validate our findings from the machine learning modelling, we used the UKB which is a large biomedical research database integrating data such as anthropometric measurements, standard biochemistry, diagnostic imaging and health records from more than 500,000 individuals recruited between 2006 and 2010 and continuously followed [
21
] (Figure
1F
). All study participants gave their informed consent at baseline, and the UKB study protocol was approved by the UK North West Multi‐centre Research Ethics Committee. For plasma proteomics, we used the data generated by Olink (Uppsala, Sweden) who have measured 2923 proteins (Olink Explore 3072 Proximity Extension Assay) expressed as Normalised Protein eXpression (NPX) units (an arbitrary and normalised unit on a log2 scale) from approximately 54,000 UKB participants' baseline visit [
22
].
We identified individuals with AIH (cases) using ICD‐10 diagnoses recorded between 1996 and February 2024. MASLD individuals were identified using ICD‐10 diagnoses and diagnostic imaging together with anthropometric measurements, medical treatment history and biochemistry, securing concurrent metabolic dysfunction as recommended by Rinella et al. [
27
]. Healthy individuals were defined as individuals without any ICD‐10 diagnoses, no signs of liver injury and not having metabolic dysfunction. This was to mimic the healthy group from our discovery cohort as much as possible. A detailed definition of diagnoses is listed in Table
S3
. Healthy and MASLD groups were collapsed into a combined control group.
As our discovery cohort consisted of newly diagnosed, untreated patients with AIH with active liver inflammation, we aimed to select AIH cases in UKB with liver inflammation at the time of proteomic analyses, i.e., at the baseline visit/recruitment. Hence, we included only AIH cases with elevated ALT levels at baseline, using a cut‐off of 45 U/L for females and 70 U/L for males, based on clinical reference values in the Capital Region, Denmark.
The Olink Explore 3072 Proximity Extension Assay measures a predefined protein list. As only a subset of the prediction proteins identified during machine learning in our discovery cohort was measured by Olink, we were not able to validate the entire plasma model. Instead, we aimed to see if the predictive proteins also measured by Olink were differentially expressed in UKB AIH cases compared with UKB controls using Wilcoxon tests and visualised with box plots. Also, multiple linear regression analyses adjusting for age and sex were performed. Analyses were performed in R version 4.3.0, and a

Introduction
Autoimmune hepatitis (AIH) is a rare immune‐mediated fibroinflammatory liver disease that is clinically challenging to diagnose as no accurate biomarker exists [
1
,
2
,
3
]. The disease has a heterogeneous presentation with a spectrum ranging from acute liver failure [
4
] to the more frequent presentations with unspecific symptoms or asymptomatic subtle chronic liver inflammation only discovered through accidental findings of elevated liver enzymes [
2
]. Consequently, one‐third of all patients with AIH, including children, have developed cirrhosis at the time of diagnosis [
5
]. As treatment with immunosuppressive medication can hamper disease progression, early and accurate diagnosing is essential.
Diagnosis of AIH is based on clinical, biochemical (particularly transaminase elevation) and serological (elevated IgG and presence of autoantibodies) findings, along with mandatory histological assessment [
1
,
2
,
6
]. However, no histological feature is pathognomonic to AIH, and the histological picture varies depending on the phenotypic presentation [
6
,
7
]. Chronic AIH is characterised by a predominantly portal‐based lymphoplasmacytic inflammation associated with interface hepatitis, and acute AIH typically reveals a lobular‐based inflammation with sparse portal/periportal histological features of chronic hepatitis. Due to morphologic overlap with viral and drug‐induced hepatitis, these etiologic factors must be excluded clinically.
Two scoring systems from the International AIH Group [
8
,
9
] strive to encompass the various diagnostic parameters to assist AIH diagnostics. The scoring systems are challenged by criteria not specific for AIH (e.g., rosette formation and emperipolesis) and are primarily based on chronic AIH [
6
]. Hence, they focus on portal/periportal inflammation, which is mainly seen in chronic AIH, as well as elevated IgG levels and detectable autoantibodies, which may be absent in acute severe AIH [
4
,
10
]. Modification of the histological criteria to address these difficulties has been proposed by the International AIH Pathology Group [
6
]. Nonetheless, they will not suffice to rule out or verify AIH with certainty, and the diverse presentations and lack of specific biomarkers make diagnosis challenging.
Another clinical difficulty lies in the differentiation between AIH and other liver diseases, particularly when conditions share overlapping clinical and biochemical features. This is especially true for diseases that present with elevated liver enzymes and hepatic steatosis on diagnostic imaging, as these findings are common in multiple liver disorders. The most important of these is metabolic dysfunction‐associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), given its high prevalence—affecting approximately 25% of the global population. There are no specific biomarkers for MASLD, making this diagnosis difficult to exclude in patients without a classical presentation of AIH. This diagnostic ambiguity also poses a problem, as patients with AIH who have metabolic syndrome could be misdiagnosed with MASLD [
11
,
12
].
Proteomics is widely used to generate insight into disease mechanism(s), biomarkers, and future treatment targets [
13
]. These methods can either focus on a preselected list of proteins (targeted) or analyse the entire detectable protein content of a sample (untargeted) [
14
], thereby producing a hypothesis‐free, unbiased dataset ideal for biomarker discovery and characterisation [
15
]. Protein profiles of patients with AIH have been assessed using micro‐array [
16
] as well as mass‐spectrometry [
17
,
18
,
19
,
20
], revealing alterations in, e.g., immune‐related proteins (polymeric immunoglobulin receptor [PIGR]), coagulation (Von Willebrand Factor [VWF]), growth factor‐binding proteins (insulin‐like growth factor [IGF]‐binding protein complex acid‐labile subunit [IGFALS]), and transport proteins (transthyretin [TTR], apolipoprotein E [APOE]).
In this study, we applied state‐of‐the‐art untargeted mass‐spectrometry‐based proteomics on both liver and plasma samples from patients with newly diagnosed, untreated AIH, MASLD and healthy individuals (discovery cohort). First, we investigated the differences between AIH and healthy, with the aim of gaining insight into AIH pathophysiology. Secondly, we used machine learning algorithms to analyse proteomics to identify biomarker panels able to distinguish AIH from not only healthy, but also MASLD. Results were validated in the United Kingdom Biobank (UKB) which is a large research resource containing targeted plasma proteomics of approximately 54,000 individuals [
21
,
22
].

3.1.2.6
Enrichment Analysis Identifies Metabolic Dysregulation in the Liver and Systemic Immune Activation of Plasma in
AIH
To better understand which biological processes, molecular functions and cellular components are altered in AIH compared with healthy controls, an enrichment analysis of the differentially expressed proteins was performed. The liver and plasma proteome uncovered distinct molecular traits. Functional analyses of the biological processes in the liver (Figure
S2
) showed a marked enhancement in protein processing, characterised by significant enrichment in ribonucleic acid (RNA) metabolism, cytoplasmic translation and protein assembly. Additionally, energy production pathways were upregulated, indicating increased metabolic activity. In contrast, plasma samples showed enrichment in immune‐related processes, including wound healing, blood coagulation, complement activation and both humoral and cellular immune responses (Figure
S3
).
Molecular function analysis of the liver (Figure
S4
) also revealed enrichment in activities related to protein synthesis and energy metabolism, as well as cellular structure (cadherin and actin binding). In the plasma, molecular functions (Figure
S5
) were enriched in enzyme activities and binding activities related to immune responses (e.g., complement and integrin binding).
Analysis of enriched cellular components in the liver (Figure
S6
) revealed enhancement of structures related to protein synthesis (e.g., ribosome) and transport (e.g., cytoplasmic vesicle lumen), as well as mitochondrial structures involved in energy metabolism. In plasma (Figure
S7
), the analysis identified components associated with the extracellular matrix, secretory pathways and various blood components (e.g., blood microparticles and lipoprotein particles). Taken together, the results from the enrichment analyses suggest that while metabolic dysregulation is a dominant feature in the liver during AIH, systemic immune activation is a hallmark of the AIH plasma proteome.

Discussion
This study is the first to describe alterations in the liver and plasma proteome of patients with newly diagnosed, untreated AIH compared with MASLD and healthy individuals. We found profound alterations of the AIH liver and plasma proteome, and that metabolic dysregulation and systemic immune activation were key features. Proteins involved in T‐cell activation and auto‐reactive antibodies were upregulated, and the IGF system was dysregulated. We also found that, in AIH, ALT and AST (enzymatically measured) consisted of the isoforms ALT1 and cAST. Both the liver and plasma proteome performed well in differentiating AIH from MASLD and healthy, demonstrating promising biomarker panels. Validation in UKB showed consistent directional changes for the proteins that were analysed in the UKB.
IGF1 and IGF2 are peptide hormones synthesised in the liver together with their binding proteins. They have insulin‐like functions, contributing to the maintenance of normal insulin sensitivity, but their main roles rely on mediating the growth‐promoting functions of growth hormone. Generally, the IGF system is considered hepatoprotective, being involved in organ development, growth and regeneration, together with involvement in lipid, protein and glucose metabolism. Treatment with systemic IGF1 in rats has shown to reduce fibrosis formation in the liver and improve liver function [
54
,
55
]. Impairment of the IGF system in chronic liver diseases like MASLD, cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma is well established [
37
] and aligns with many of our findings in AIH, although MASLD has been associated with increased levels of IGFBP3 [
56
].
In AIH, potential dysregulation of the IGF system remains unexplored. We identified consistent downregulation of IGF1, IGF2, IGFBP3 and IGFALS in AIH compared with both healthy controls and MASLD. Interestingly, these alterations were attenuated after exclusion of patients with cirrhosis in the AIH versus MASLD comparison but remained evident when comparing AIH with healthy controls. One possible explanation is that the IGF system may be more closely associated with fibrotic processes rather than cirrhosis alone. In our cohort, both the AIH and MASLD groups exhibited varying degrees of fibrosis (53% with F1─F3 fibrosis and 65% with F1─F2 fibrosis, respectively; Table
S5
), but cirrhosis was more prevalent in AIH (26%) than MASLD (6%) (Table
1
and Table
S5
). Thus, when comparing AIH with healthy controls, who had no fibrosis and no cirrhosis, the IGF system alterations persisted, whereas the fibrosis burden between AIH and MASLD was more similar after excluding cirrhosis, potentially explaining the loss of significance. However, our study was not sufficiently powered to adjust for fibrosis stage in the analyses. The disruptions in the IGF system in patients with AIH, observed in our study, could also be associated with the well‐known disturbances of glucose metabolism observed in these patients [
57
,
58
,
59
]. While these findings highlight potential dysregulation of the IGF system in AIH, functional validation through mechanistic studies or targeted assays in independent patient cohorts would be necessary to confirm these results and elucidate their biological relevance.
ALT and AST are found in different organs within the body, with the highest concentration observed in the liver. They are both considered tissue leakage proteins, normally present in the blood in low concentrations, but with rising levels upon tissue damage. ALT1 has been localised to the cytosol and endoplasmic reticulum in human hepatocytes, whereas ALT2 has been localised to the mitochondria and endoplasmic reticulum of human skeletal muscle cells [
60
]. Our study confirms previous findings that upon liver inflammation, increased leakage of ALT1 but not ALT2 to the blood is observed, whereas leakage of ALT2 occurs in other situations such as muscle injury [
61
,
62
]. In rats, leakage of cAST preceded that of mAST during liver ischemia, suggesting mAST was leaked to the blood only after severe damage of hepatocytes [
63
]. This might explain our finding of increased cAST, but not mAST, in plasma. Our findings of an almost perfect correlation between enzymatically measured ALT and ALT1 together with AST and cAST underscore that mass spectrometry concentrations are accurate, although relative, underlining the validity of proteomics. It also suggests that isoform‐specific measurements could be relevant in distinguishing liver‐derived enzyme elevations from those originating in other tissues, offering potential diagnostic value in clinical practice.
Previous proteomic studies in AIH are scarce. Early studies (2004─2012) used mass spectrometry to identify a few selected proteins using gel electrophoresis techniques [
16
,
64
,
65
,
66
,
67
,
68
]. More recently, serum proteomics have been done in adult patients with AIH cirrhosis (2019) [
18
] and paediatric patients with AIH (2023) [
17
], and saliva proteomics have been performed in adult AIH cohorts (2023) [
19
,
20
]. When aiming for the identification of novel biomarkers, these studies have some limitations, though. First, when evaluating diagnostics, it is a concern that the cohorts were not restricted to newly diagnosed or untreated patients with AIH. Diagnostic biomarkers assessed after treatment are likely to be attenuated after immunosuppressive medication is initiated. Secondly, the studies included healthy individuals as control groups, which may not be ideal in biomarker discovery as findings may not be AIH specific but could indicate, e.g., liver inflammation in general. Regarding liver proteomics, only one study has, to our knowledge, been performed in a small cohort of AIH explant livers (2011) [
69
].
Minghui et al. [
18
] conducted an untargeted serum proteomics experiment in 16 patients with AIH cirrhosis and 16 sex‐matched healthy controls, identifying 108 differentially expressed proteins in AIH cirrhosis (
p
< 0.05 and an FDR < 0.01). Several of those were also observed in our study, including increased levels of VWF, PIGR, IGHG1 and C7 and decreased levels of TTR, IGFALS, APOE, apolipoprotein A1 (APOA1), inter‐alpha‐trypsin inhibitor heavy chain H1 (ITIH1), vitamin K‐dependent protein C (PROC) and C8B. Using a panel of eight proteins (VWF, TTR, IGFALS, APOE, adiponectin [ADIPO] PIGR, gelsolin [GELS]), Minghui et al. achieved a ROC AUC of 1.00 (95% confidence interval 1.00─1.00) in discriminating AIH cirrhosis from healthy controls. Evaluation by Western blot in a larger cohort (90 patients with AIH cirrhosis, 90 patients with non‐cirrhotic AIH, 120 controls) confirmed these alterations, although they were less pronounced in non‐cirrhotic AIH, except for PIGR, which showed greater increases in non‐cirrhotic AIH compared with AIH cirrhosis. Of their predictive proteins, TTR, VWF and IGFALS were also identified as key predictive proteins in our plasma models. Particularly, TTR was the most important predictor in classifying AIH from healthy and MASLD, irrespective of cirrhosis or not.
TTR has primarily been associated with amyloidosis as misfolded TTR proteins can aggregate into amyloid fibrils [
70
]. However, downregulation of TTR, as observed in AIH in our study, may also reflect alterations in Vitamin A homeostasis. TTR is primarily produced in the liver and transports thyroxine hormone and Vitamin A (retinol), the latter by forming a complex with RBP4. Vitamin A is involved in the maintenance of growth and vision, systemic metabolic regulation, herein lipid and carbohydrate metabolism, and plays regulatory roles in innate and adaptive immune responses [
71
,
72
]. Dietary Vitamin A is taken up by hepatocytes and primarily stored in lipid droplets in quiescent hepatic stellate cells. Upon activation during liver injury, hepatic stellate cells differentiate into activated myofibroblasts and lose their Vitamin A storage, underscoring the well‐known association of Vitamin A deficiency and fibrosis formation in chronic liver disease [
73
,
74
]. Downregulation of TTR is not specific for AIH and has also been observed in MASLD [
75
] and alcohol‐related liver disease [
76
]. Nevertheless, downregulation of TTR was more pronounced in AIH in our study (FC TTR plasma and liver < 0.70 in AIH versus MASLD). This may be explained by Vitamin A's involvement in immune system regulation [
72
] in addition to involvement in lipid metabolism and fibrosis [
71
,
73
].
The pattern of more pronounced alterations of the plasma proteome in cirrhosis found by Minghui et al. [
18
] is consistent with findings from our study and has also been observed in MASLD [
75
] and alcohol‐related liver disease [
76
]. Clinically, this aligns with the phenotypical presentation as non‐cirrhotic liver damage is often asymptomatic, while cirrhosis frequently manifests with observable alterations like sarcopenia, ascites, gynaecomastia and splenomegaly.
The lower ROC AUC of the plasma model found in our study (0.91) compared to Minghui et al. [
18
] (1.00) may result from methodological differences and cohort composition. Our repeated stratified cross‐validation approach minimises overfitting and better accounts for variability, while their single ROC analysis might overestimate performance. Additionally, Minghui et al. [
18
] used healthy controls, likely more distinct from AIH patients, whereas our control group included both healthy individuals and MASLD patients, providing a more clinically relevant but challenging classification scenario.
Serum proteomics has also been performed in paediatric patients with AIH by Sîrbe et al. [
17
]. They recruited 16 prevalent patients with AIH and 2 newly diagnosed patients with decompensated AIH cirrhosis and compared their serum proteomic profile with 18 age‐ and sex‐matched healthy individuals using two 92‐target panels (inflammation and cardiometabolic) from Olink. They did not observe any significant alterations at an adjusted
P
level. This may be a consequence of studying the plasma proteome of patients already receiving medical treatment, which aims to normalise the condition, together with the use of targeted proteomics, only studying a pre‐selected list of proteins, undoubtedly overlooking potential interesting alterations.
4.1
Strengths and Limitations
Our study has several notable strengths. First, the inclusion of liver tissue from not only AIH patients but also healthy individuals and patients with MASLD allowed us to identify disease‐specific alterations. Secondly, combining liver and plasma proteomics offered a unique opportunity to trace liver‐specific alterations in plasma. As plasma reflects processes from across the body—and is influenced by various comorbidities—disease‐specific changes in plasma can be difficult to identify and often require large sample sizes [
77
]. By combining tissue and plasma proteomics, we were able to identify disease‐specific changes in plasma. Importantly, our study included newly diagnosed, untreated patients with AIH, which is particularly valuable for biomarker discovery, as diagnostic biomarkers are most relevant prior to treatment initiation. Additionally, by sharing our dataset, including data on all the differentially expressed proteins, we enable other researchers to explore and validate their own hypotheses.
A limitation of our study is the lack of age and sex matching in the discovery cohort (AIH group was older and a higher proportion of females), and we cannot leave out that some observed changes may be influenced by these factors. A systematic review by Johnson et al. [
78
] identified 32 proteins that change significantly with age, reported in at least five studies. Of the proteins reported in our study, only albumin and cAST were identified as age‐specific proteins in the review. Since albumin and cAST are known to vary due to liver disease, we do not believe these changes are primarily age‐related in our study. Also, cAST, which was one of the proteins in our plasma model validated in UKB, remained significantly increased in the validation cohort in UKB after adjusting for age and sex.
Although previous proteomics studies have observed sex differences in serum/plasma protein levels, findings are inconsistent [
79
,
80
]. For example, SAA1 [
79
] and B2M [
80
], both of which are involved in inflammation and immune response and elevated in AIH in our discovery cohort, have been reported at higher levels in females than in males. Potential sex‐related differences in the human liver proteome remain unexplored.
To address this limitation, we also performed sensitivity analyses adjusting for age and sex in our discovery cohort. Several proteins, including B2M as mentioned above, remained significantly altered after adjustment, suggesting that these findings are not solely driven by demographic differences.
Another limitation of our study is the lack of identification of low abundant peptides, like chemokines, which play roles in immune diseases like AIH [
28
]. This underrepresentation derives from the sensitivity in untargeted proteomics, where detection tends to favour highly abundant proteins. In biological samples, proteins span a wide range of concentrations and sizes, and low abundant proteins are often missed.
A limitation of our validation in UKB is the use of targeted Olink proteomics, which measures a preselected list of proteins, unlike our untargeted approach. Consequently, many immune‐mediated predictive proteins from our plasma model were not included in the Olink panel, limiting our ability to fully validate the plasma model in UKB. Additionally, our sample sizes in both the discovery and validation cohorts were small, highlighting the need for further validation in larger cohorts.
5
Conclusions
In this study, we conducted the first parallel characterisation of the liver and plasma proteome in newly diagnosed, untreated AIH patients. Using an untargeted approach, we found profound alterations of both the liver and plasma proteome and promising diagnostic biomarker panels with good diagnostic accuracy. Sensitivity analyses adjusting for age and sex confirmed that several key proteomic differences, including immune‐related proteins, were not solely driven by demographic differences. Our findings have potential to improve the diagnostic work‐up of patients suspected of having AIH. To confirm our findings and refine the panels, we plan to perform liver and plasma proteomics on larger, age‐ and sex‐matched cohorts.
